definition: Cleave means to divide something into parts.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cleave. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cleave should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The butcher's heavy blade can cleave a whole side of beef into matched halves with a single stroke.
Crack is milder than cleave — a cracked block carries a line of damage but still holds together as one piece, while a cleaved one has come apart into clean, separate parts.
Shatter goes further than cleave: not two clean halves but a hundred useless fragments flying apart.

Split is the everyday word for dividing something along a line — you split firewood, a bill, a sandwich. Cleave is the vivid, slightly literary cousin: it suggests one decisive blow, often along a natural seam, leaving clean whole pieces. Anything cleaved is split, but cleave adds drama and precision.

Sunder is literary and violent: to tear something apart, often people or bonds, and usually for good. Cleave is calmer and more exact — a clean division into parts, often at a single stroke along a natural line. Sundering wrenches things apart; cleaving splits them cleanly.

Cleave is vivid and slightly literary: reach for it when something is divided cleanly into parts at one decisive blow, or when a group splits for good.
One warning — English has a second, unrelated verb cleave meaning to cling ('she cleaved to her beliefs'), so let context make clear you mean splitting.
Compare truncate, this unit's word for cutting short: cleaving divides a thing into parts; truncating merely lops off its end.

The demonstration that closed the tournament belonged to Master Ito, who set out a stack of pine boards and asked the audience a single question: where does wood want to break?
She turned the top board so its grain ran straight toward the crowd, set it across two blocks, then raised one hand.
The strike came down and seemed to cleave the board almost gently, the two halves dropping away with edges as smooth as if they had been sawn.
A guest who tried the same blow across the grain got only splinters and a bruised palm.
Force matters, Ito told her students afterward, but the clean stroke is the one that follows the seam the wood already offers.
